turns.text: Welcome to Lesson 9.1: From Fundamentals to Advanced Data Collection! Classical dataset collection operates under static batch boundaries: periodic SQL exports, fixed web snapshots, or offline questionnaires. Modern production AI runs continuously and unbounded across 100 kilohertz IoT meshes, distributed commit logs, and human-in-the-loop crowdsourcing markets.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Today we derive the four mathematical physics laws protecting continuous acquisition pipelines: the Shannon-Hartley channel capacity margin, Little's Law and finite M/M/1/K reactive backpressure, the batch-versus-streaming small-files amortization frontier, and IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol sensor synchronization.

slides.title: Definition 9.1.1: Shannon-Hartley Channel Capacity & Margin

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Definition 9.1.1: Shannon-Hartley Channel Capacity & Margin

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Our first physical law is the Shannon-Hartley Theorem from 1948. For a noisy cellular uplink or RF fieldbus with analog carrier bandwidth B in hertz and linear signal-to-noise power ratio S over N equals 10 to the SNR decibels divided by 10, maximum error-free channel capacity C equals B times log base 2 of 1 plus S over N.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Take a concrete edge link: B equals 2.0 megahertz at 15 decibels SNR, giving linear S over N equal to 31.6228 and channel capacity C equal to 10.056 megabits per second. If sensors emit 2,500 events per second at 600 bytes—or 4,800 bits per event—demanded ingress R_ingest hits 12.000 megabits per second! Margin delta C drops to negative 1.944 megabits per second, guaranteeing irreversible packet loss unless payloads are compressed at the edge.

solo.contentHtml:
Shannon-Hartley Capacity & Ingestion Stability Margin

Def 9.1.1 • Shannon (1948)
$$C = B \log_2\left(1 + \frac{S}{N}\right), \qquad \frac{S}{N} = 10^{\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / 10}$$ $$R_{\text{ingest}} = \lambda \cdot b_{\text{evt}} = \lambda \cdot 8|e|_{\text{bytes}} \lt C, \qquad \Delta C = C - R_{\text{ingest}} \gt 0$$
1. Physical Bound ($B=2\text{ MHz}$)
$C \approx 10.056\text{ Mbps}$

At $15\text{ dB}$, linear $\frac{S}{N} = 10^{1.5} \approx 31.6228$; $\log_2(32.6228) \approx 5.0278\text{ bits/Hz}$.

2. Raw Stream Demand
$R_{\text{ingest}} = 12.000\text{ Mbps}$

$\lambda = 2{,}500\text{ evt/s} \times 600\text{ B}$ ($4{,}800\text{ bits/evt}$).

3. Link Saturation Deficit
$\Delta C = -1.944\text{ Mbps}$

Violates $R_{\text{ingest}} \lt C$: physical-layer socket drops unless compressed at edge.

duo.speaker: Socratic Debate (Dr. Nova & Kaito)
duo.title: Socratic Debate: Why No TCP Buffer Fixes a Saturated Shannon Pipe

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Hold on, Dr. Nova—if my edge gateway demands 12 megabits per second over a 10.056-megabit wireless channel, can't TCP congestion control just buffer packets briefly until the burst passes?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Not for sustained streams, Kaito! Shannon's theorem establishes an information-theoretic ceiling of 10.056 megabits per second at 2 megahertz and 15 decibels. Any excess 1.944 megabits per second cannot cross the RF channel error-free. No software retry loop creates extra spectrum—you must deploy edge delta compression or adaptive frame pruning!

$C = 10.056\text{ Mbps}$

$15\text{ dB} \implies \frac{S}{N} = 31.6228$; absolute error-free physical rate limit.

$2{,}500\text{ evt/s} \times 4{,}800\text{ bits/evt}$ ($600\text{ B}$ raw frames).

Hard Remedy Required
$\Delta C = -1.944\text{ Mbps}$

TCP retries only inflate latency; compress or drop stale redundancy at edge.

slides.title: Definition 9.1.2a: Little's Law & Tail Residency Blowup

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Definition 9.1.2a: Little's Law & Tail Residency Blowup

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Even when the physical RF uplink has generous Shannon margin, ingestion brokers still fail inside RAM! Little's Law proves that in any stationary queue, mean in-flight buffer concurrency L equals effective admitted throughput lambda_eff multiplied by expected residency or commit latency W—regardless of arrival distribution.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Look at why tail stalls are lethal: at 50,000 events per second with a healthy 20-millisecond commit time, L holds 1,000 events. But if a downstream disk fsync stall stretches latency W from 10 milliseconds to 500 milliseconds, buffer occupancy explodes fifty times instantaneously! That is why a 2,500-event-per-second gateway with 80-millisecond latency—yielding L equals 200 baseline—must still provision 3x to 5x burst headroom.

solo.contentHtml:
Little's Law In-Flight Concurrency & Commit Tail Stalls

Def 9.1.2a • Little (1961)
$$L = \lambda_{\text{eff}} \cdot W$$
High-Velocity Gateway
$L = 1{,}000\text{ events}$

At $\lambda = 50{,}000\text{ evt/s}$ and $W = 20\text{ ms}$ ($0.02\text{ s}$) broker residency.

Disk Fsync Stall Blowup
$50\times\text{ RAM Spike}$

Commit latency jumping $10\text{ ms} \to 500\text{ ms}$ multiplies $L$ linearly into OOM danger.

Buffer Provisioning Rule
$L=200 \implies \ge 1{,}000\text{ slots}$

At $2{,}500 \times 0.08\text{ s} = 200$ baseline, allocate $3\times$–$5\times$ transient burst headroom.

duo.speaker: Socratic Debate (Dr. Nova & Kaito)
duo.title: Socratic Debate: Why Steady-State Concurrency Fails Under Burst Tails

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: So if Little's Law gives L equals 2,500 times 0.08 seconds—just 200 concurrent events in RAM—can I size my gateway consumer queue strictly to 200 slots to save memory?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Dangerous trap, Kaito! 200 is merely the stationary expectation. The moment downstream storage hits a garbage-collection pause or disk fsync stall—say 10 milliseconds jumping to 500 milliseconds—occupancy inflates 50 times! Always provision 3x to 5x burst headroom plus reactive flow control.

duo.contentHtml:
Little's Law In-Flight Concurrency & Commit Tail Stalls

Def 9.1.2a • Little (1961)
$$L = \lambda_{\text{eff}} \cdot W \qquad (\text{Distribution-Independent Invariant})$$
50k/s Benchmark
$L = 1{,}000\text{ events}$

$50{,}000 \times 0.02\text{ s}$ steady in-flight backlog.

Fsync Stall Multiplier
$10\text{ ms} \to 500\text{ ms} \;(50\times)$

Latency spikes immediately multiply RAM occupancy.

3x–5x Headroom Rule
$L=200 \to \ge 1{,}000\text{ slots}$

Never provision strictly at mean $L$; cushion transient bursts.

slides.title: Definition 9.1.2b: Finite M/M/1/K Overflow & Token-Bucket Control

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Definition 9.1.2b: Finite M/M/1/K Overflow & Token-Bucket Control

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Real brokers have finite memory K slots. Modeling the consumer queue as a Markovian M/M/1/K buffer with worker service capacity mu and traffic intensity rho equal to lambda over mu yields the exact steady-state overflow drop probability P_drop of K: 1 over K plus 1 at rho equals 1, and 1 minus rho times rho to the K divided by 1 minus rho to the K plus 1 otherwise.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Observe the sharp phase transition at K equals 20 and mu equals 1,000 events per second! Under steady traffic lambda 800—rho 0.80—drop loss is barely 0.233 percent. Under a 25-percent burst to lambda 1,250—rho 1.25—unthrottled packet eviction jumps to 20.19 percent! Engaging Token-Bucket Reactive Backpressure at rho_cap 0.90 caps intake at 900 events per second, shedding 350 deterministically via HTTP 429 or Kafka pause and cutting queue loss down to 1.38 percent.

solo.contentHtml:
Finite $M/M/1/K$ Overflow & Token-Bucket Reactive Backpressure

Def 9.1.2b • Wang et al. (2015)
$$P_{\text{drop}}(K) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{K + 1} & \text{if } \rho = 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{(1 - \rho)\,\rho^K}{1 - \rho^{K+1}} & \text{if } \rho \ne 1 \end{cases}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{admit}} = \min(\lambda, \rho_{\text{cap}}\mu), \quad \lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda_{\text{admit}}(1 - P_{\text{drop}})$$
Steady ($\lambda=800, \rho=0.80$)
$P_{\text{drop}}(20) = 0.233\%$

At $K=20, \mu=1{,}000$, sub-1.0 utilization holds tail overflow negligible.

Unthrottled Burst ($\rho=1.25$)
$P_{\text{drop}}(20) = 20.19\%$

$\lambda=1{,}250$ evicts $\sim 252.4\text{ evt/s}$ silently (or triggers OOM crashes).

Token Bucket ($\rho_{\text{cap}}=0.90$)
$P_{\text{drop}}(20) = 1.38\%$

Admits $900\text{ evt/s}$, signals HTTP 429 / Kafka pause() on $350\text{ evt/s}$.

duo.speaker: Socratic Debate (Dr. Nova & Kaito)
duo.title: Socratic Debate: Silent Broker Eviction vs. Explicit HTTP 429 Backpressure

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: Wait a second, Nova—with Token-Bucket Reactive Backpressure at rho_cap 0.90 during a 1,250-event-per-second burst, I'm rejecting 350 events per second at the door! Isn't rejection just another form of data loss?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Huge operational distinction, Kaito! Silent eviction inside an unthrottled M/M/1/20 queue corrupts 20.19 percent indiscriminately—including your highest-value safety anomalies—or triggers an OOM kernel kill! Deterministic HTTP 429 or Kafka consumer pause lets smart edge producers buffer in flash memory, retry, and protect core broker residency.

Finite $M/M/1/K$ Overflow & Token-Bucket Reactive Backpressure

Def 9.1.2b • Wang et al. (2015)
$$P_{\text{drop}}(K) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{K + 1} & \text{if } \rho = 1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{(1 - \rho)\,\rho^K}{1 - \rho^{K+1}} & \text{if } \rho \ne 1 \end{cases}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{admit}} = \min(\lambda, 0.90\mu)$$

slides.title: Definition 9.1.3: Batch vs. Stream Latency & Small-Files Amortization

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Definition 9.1.3: Batch vs. Stream Latency & Small-Files Amortization

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Our third theoretical formulation compares Batch versus Streaming Latency alongside the Small-Files Amortization Frontier. Accumulating 10,000 events of 500 bytes across a 60-second batch window over a 100-megabit link gives batch latency T_batch equal to 60.40 seconds. Streaming a single event with 5-millisecond processing time achieves T_stream equal to 5.04 milliseconds—an 11,984-times speedup!

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Why don't we flush every streaming event individually to S3 or Google Cloud Storage? Because object-store catalog overhead C_meta causes the Small Files Problem! Flushing every 100 milliseconds writes 36,000 tiny files per hour, driving metadata tax tau_meta upward. Production Kappa and Lakehouse architectures run dual paths: sub-10-millisecond streaming for online serving plus asynchronous compaction into 128-megabyte Parquet partitions delivering 5x to 10x higher scan throughput.

solo.contentHtml:
Latency Differential & Object-Store Small-Files Amortization

Def 9.1.3 • Zaharia (2016)
$$T_{\text{batch}} = \Delta t_{\text{batch}} + \frac{8 N_b |e|}{B_{\text{net}}}, \qquad T_{\text{stream}} = t_{\text{proc}} + \frac{8 |e|}{B_{\text{net}}}, \qquad \text{Speedup} = \frac{T_{\text{batch}}}{T_{\text{stream}}}$$ $$N_{\text{files/hr}} = \frac{3600}{\Delta t_{\text{flush}}}, \qquad \tau_{\text{meta}}(\Delta t_{\text{flush}}) = \frac{C_{\text{meta}}}{\lambda \cdot \Delta t_{\text{flush}} \cdot |e|}$$
1. Latency Speedup
$11{,}984\times$ Faster

$T_{\text{batch}}=60.40\text{ s}$ ($N_b=10{,}000$) vs. $T_{\text{stream}}=5.04\text{ ms}$ ($100\text{ Mbps}$).

2. Small-Files Tax
$36{,}000\text{ files/hr}$

Naive $100\text{ ms}$ flushes swamp S3/GCS PUT/LIST & catalog metadata.

3. Kappa / Lakehouse Tier
$128\text{ MB}$ Parquet

Async Iceberg/Delta compaction yields $5\times$–$10\times$ higher compression & scan speed.

duo.speaker: Socratic Debate (Dr. Nova & Kaito)
duo.title: Socratic Debate: Resolving the 11,984x Latency vs. Small-Files Paradox

turns.speaker: Kaito
turns.text: 60.40 seconds versus 5.04 milliseconds—that's nearly a 12,000-times observation speedup! Why shouldn't our streaming Flink jobs commit tiny Parquet files to cloud storage every 100 milliseconds so analysts see live data immediately?

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Do the file arithmetic, Kaito: 3,600 divided by 0.1 seconds produces 36,000 tiny files per hour—nearly a million objects per day per partition! Catalog LIST lookups and Parquet footer reads overwhelm actual scan compute, and you lose cross-partition end-of-day joins. Dual-path Kappa/Lakehouse serves millisecond streams in Kafka while compacting 128-megabyte Parquet stripes in the background.

duo.contentHtml:
Latency Differential & Object-Store Small-Files Amortization

Def 9.1.3 • Kleppmann (2017)
$$\text{Speedup} = \frac{60.40\text{ s}}{5.04\text{ ms}} = 11{,}984\times, \qquad \tau_{\text{meta}}(\Delta t_{\text{flush}}) = \frac{C_{\text{meta}}}{\lambda \cdot \Delta t_{\text{flush}} \cdot |e|}$$
Hot Path: Online Serving
$< 10\text{ ms}$ via Kafka

$t_{\text{proc}}=5\text{ ms} + 0.04\text{ ms}$ wire time for $500\text{ B}$ event @ $100\text{ Mbps}$.

Anti-Pattern: $100\text{ ms}$ S3 Flush
$36{,}000\text{ tiny files/hr}$

Catalog metadata latency $C_{\text{meta}}$ eclipses data payload scan.

Cold Path: Compaction
$128\text{ MB}$ Stripes + Joins

class AdvancedIngestionEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_shannon_channel(bandwidth_hz: float, snr_db: float, arrival_rate_hz: float, event_bytes: int):
        cap_bps = bandwidth_hz * math.log2(1.0 + 10.0 ** (snr_db / 10.0))
        demand_bps = arrival_rate_hz * event_bytes * 8.0
        return ChannelCapacityReport(..., capacity_mbps=round(cap_bps/1e6, 4), is_stable=demand_bps < cap_bps)

    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_mm1k_queue(arrival_rate_hz: float, service_rate_hz: float, k: int, w_sec: float, bp_cap: float = 0.0):
        admitted = min(arrival_rate_hz, bp_cap * service_rate_hz) if bp_cap > 0.0 else arrival_rate_hz
        rho = admitted / service_rate_hz
        p_drop = 1.0/(k+1) if math.isclose(rho, 1.0) else ((1-rho)*rho**k)/(1-rho**(k+1))
        eff = admitted * (1.0 - p_drop)
        return QueueBackpressureReport(utilization_rho=rho, p_drop_unthrottled=p_drop, inflight_backlog_l=eff*w_sec, ...)

    @staticmethod
    def compare_batch_vs_stream(event_bytes: int, n_batch: int, batch_sec: float, net_bps: float, proc_sec: float = 0.005):
        t_batch = batch_sec + (event_bytes * n_batch * 8.0 / net_bps)
        t_stream = proc_sec + (event_bytes * 8.0 / net_bps)
        return LatencyTradeoffReport(batch_latency_sec=t_batch, stream_latency_sec=t_stream, speedup_ratio=t_batch/t_stream, ...)

    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_sensor_sync(timestamps_sec: List[float], velocity_mps: float):
        arr = np.asarray(timestamps_sec, dtype=float)
        skew_sec = float(np.max(arr) - np.min(arr))
        return SensorSyncReport(jitter_ms=float(np.std(arr)*1000), spatial_drift_m=velocity_mps*skew_sec, ptp_compliant=(skew_sec*1000)<=1.0)

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Our Pydantic V2 CrowdsourcingEngine verifies every claim numerically: 82.83 percent at n=9, 93.96 percent at n=25, crossing 95.24 percent at n=29, exact Fleiss' Kappa scores of 0.4444 versus 0.7321, and Dawid-Skene rescuing Class 1 from a 2-to-1 adversarial majority loss.

solo.contentHtml:
Production Consensus Suite (Pydantic V2): Python 3.10+ 
class CrowdsourcingEngine:
    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_condorcet(n_workers: int, worker_accuracy: float) -> CondorcetReport:
        m = (n_workers - 1) // 2
        prob = sum(math.comb(n_workers, k) * (worker_accuracy**k) * ((1 - worker_accuracy)**(n_workers - k))
                   for k in range(m + 1, n_workers + 1))
        return CondorcetReport(n_workers=n_workers, majority_accuracy=round(prob, 6), ...)

    @staticmethod
    def select_active_learning_queries(probabilities: np.ndarray, top_k: int = 1) -> ActiveQueryReport:
        p = np.clip(probabilities, 1e-12, 1.0)
        entropies = -np.sum(p * np.log2(p), axis=1)
        return ActiveQueryReport(selected_indices=np.argsort(entropies)[::-1][:top_k].tolist(), ...)

    @staticmethod
    def evaluate_dawid_skene_and_budget(priors, worker_confusions, votes, ...):
        # Inverts systematic flippers (p=0.15) cleanly using log-odds confusion likelihoods
        log_posts = {c: math.log(q_c) + sum(math.log(conf[(c, v)]) for conf, v in zip(worker_confusions, votes))
                     for c, q_c in priors.items()}
◆

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Three equations govern platform operations. First, true hourly earnings divide reward by both active completion time and unpaid queue-search latency, explaining Hara et al.'s 2 dollar MTurk median wage. Second, 5 four-choice honeypot traps give a 1-in-1024 false-pass rate of 0.0977 percent. Third, Weibull retention reveals burnout rising past hour 4.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Conceptual Overview & Derivation: The Mathematics of the Dawid-Skene Expectation-Maximization Model. Formalizing the empirical sample mathematically reveals that empirical risk only approximates true generalization risk when the i.i.d. assumption holds. When upstream sampling is biased, the empirical risk diverges asymptotically from true risk—no model tuning can fix that.

solo.contentHtml:
📐 Mathematical Formulation Empirical Sample Formulation
$$\Pr(Z_i = k \mid \mathbf{Y}_i) = \frac{p_k \prod_{w \in \mathcal{W}_i} \pi_{k, Y_{iw}}^{(w)}}{\sum_{j=1}^K p_j \prod_{w \in \mathcal{W}_i} \pi_{j, Y_{iw}}^{(w)}}$$
📐 Mathematical Formulation Distribution Measure
$$\hat{\pi}_{k, \ell}^{(w)} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_w} \mathbb{I}(Y_{iw} = \ell) \cdot \Pr(Z_i = k \mid \mathbf{Y}_i)}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_w} \Pr(Z_i = k \mid \mathbf{Y}_i)}$$
📐 Mathematical Formulation Empirical Risk Proxy
$$\hat{p}_k = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \Pr(Z_i = k \mid \mathbf{Y}_i)$$
💡 Industrial Best Practice Adopt the Partnership on AI guidelines for crowdsourced data work: guarantee living wages based on median completion times, provide transparent feedback on rejected tasks, and implement psychological support for workers reviewing toxic content.
◆
Ensuring high data quality across platforms and behavioral panels ((Peer et al., 2022)) requires statistical quality modeling to disentangle genuine worker skill from task difficulty ((Snow et al., 2008)), measuring inter-coder consensus ((Artstein & Poesio, 2008)), while adhering strictly to ethical labor standards regarding fair pay, informed consent, and psychological welfare ((Ipeirotis et al., 2010)).
▸
In real-world crowdsourcing simple majority voting fails when worker reliability varies widely.
⚡
To prevent worker exploitation, the task reward $R$ must satisfy: Rejection of worker submissions without specific, auditable rationale is prohibited under responsible AI governance frameworks ((Kittur et al., 2013)).

import numpy as np
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

class DawidSkeneAggregator:
    """Implements Dawid-Skene EM algorithm for crowdsourced label aggregation."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes: int = 2):
        self.K = n_classes

    def run_em(self, responses: List[Tuple[int, int, int]], max_iter: int = 50, tol: float = 1e-4) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, dict]:
        """Runs Dawid-Skene EM algorithm.
        
        Args:
            responses: List of (item_id, worker_id, label) tuples.
        """

Formalizing the empirical sample mathematically reveals that empirical risk only approximates true generalization risk when the i.i.d. assumption holds. When upstream sampling is biased, the empirical risk diverges asymptotically from true risk—no model tuning can fix that.

solo.speaker: Dr. Nova (Senior Architect)
solo.title: Conceptual Overview & Derivation: The Mathematics of Columnar Projection & Bin-Packing Compaction

turns.speaker: Dr. Nova
turns.text: Conceptual Overview & Derivation: The Mathematics of Columnar Projection & Bin-Packing Compaction. Formalizing the empirical sample mathematically reveals that empirical risk only approximates true generalization risk when the i.i.d. assumption holds. When upstream sampling is biased, the empirical risk diverges asymptotically from true risk—no model tuning can fix that.

solo.contentHtml:
📐 Mathematical Formulation Empirical Sample Formulation
$$R_{\text{IO}} = \frac{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{Q}} \text{size}(A_j)}{\sum_{j=1}^M \text{size}(A_j)}$$
📐 Mathematical Formulation Distribution Measure
$$\mathcal{S}_{\text{compaction}} = \frac{N_{\text{micro}} \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{net}}}}{\left\lceil \frac{V}{S_{\text{target}}} \right\rceil \cdot t_{\text{req}} + \frac{V}{B_{\text{net}}}}$$
📐 Mathematical Formulation Empirical Risk Proxy
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{comp}} = |\Sigma| \cdot \ell_{\text{dict}} + N \cdot \lceil \log_2 |\Sigma| \rceil$$
💡 Industrial Best Practice Adopt Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake as your table format. Iceberg provides full ACID transactions, hidden partitioning (query engines auto-prune partitions without users hardcoding partition columns), and schema evolution without rewriting petabytes o
◆
Historically, enterprise data collection was split between two disparate systems: structured relational data warehouses (fast SQL, but expensive and unable to store unstructured tensors) and unstructured cloud data lakes rooted in distributed filesystems like HDFS ((Shvachko et al., 2010)) and message backbones ((Wang et al., 2015)) (cheap S3 storage, but lacking ACID transactions and suffering from data quality rot) ((Armbrust et al., 2020)).
▸
The Data Lakehouse architecture unifies both paradigms, implementing transaction logs, schema enforcement, and time-travel querying powered by unified compute engines ((Zaharia et al., 2016)) and decentralized Data Mesh ownership ((Dehghani, 2022)) directly on top of open columnar Parquet files ((Nambiar & Mundra, 2022)).
⚡
Columnar blocks achieve high compression ratios through dictionary and run-length encoding (RLE).
💡
When $|\Sigma| \ll N$, dictionary encoding compresses dense string columns by up to $90\%$.
